name: Stack and versions in the summary sidebar

pr.title: List the pull requests in a summary's stack in its sidebar
pr.head: 3710a64b15a0fb228c8909050283eef67d2ff1e6

summary: A Projector site serves one summary page per pull request: a guided walk through its diff, with a sidebar that names the pull request and lists the page's sections. When pull requests are stacked, each one based on the branch of the one before, a reviewer works through them in order, but a summary page named only its own pull request, so moving to the next one meant going back to the Reviews list.

This change lists every pull request in the stack in the sidebar, below the repo#number header: the ones beneath this pull request down to the default branch, and every one stacked above any of them. Each row shows the number and title and links to that pull request's summary, and the current row is highlighted. It also drops the sidebar line of head commit, base branch, and files link, which repeated the page header, and moves Versions below the sections as a list that starts closed, one line per published head with when it was published.

The stack is worked out when the site deploys, from every summary stored on refs/projector/summaries, so a page learns of a pull request stacked on it later without being republished, and the deploy asks GitHub nothing new.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Stack: pull requests where each one's base branch is the head branch of another open pull request.
  • Base: the pull request directly beneath one in its stack. stack_bases maps each stacked pull request to its base.
  • Head or version: one published commit of a pull request. A summary is stored per head, and the page for a pull request shows its newest.
  • Payload: the JSON a page loads, written by the deploy as data.json beside each page.

cards.title: What it leaves alone
cards.html:
• The Reviews index still marks a stacked pull request with "Stacked on #N"; only its source of stackedOn moved.
  • A page built on its own, by project site page or as an Artifact, has no other summaries to read, so it has no stack and keeps the single title line.
  • Pull requests in a stack that never got a summary appear only when another summary names them as its base, and then with a number and no title.

groups.title: Working out each page's stack at deploy time
groups.kicker: The deploy computes the stack once and writes it into every page's data.
intro: The site deploy reads every summary on the summaries ref and writes each page's data.json. Before this change it wrote those pages first and only afterwards worked out which pull request sits on which, for the Reviews index. Now build_summaries works out the bases before it writes any page, so each page can carry its stack.

stack_rows turns the bases into one page's list: it walks down from the current pull request to the bottom of its stack, then lists that bottom pull request and everything stacked above it, depth first, each pull request's own branches after it, lowest number first.

checks.text: The bases come from the newest head of each pull request, because a pull request retargeted to main after its base merged records the new base only in the summary of its newer head.

files.note: Computes the bases inside build_summaries, adds stack_rows, and has build_site reuse each entry's stackedOn.

checks.text: prs holds each pull request's newest pr record. The loop below already uses newest for the newest head's SHA, which is why this map has another name.

The build still asks GitHub about each base branch at most once: stack_bases runs here a single time, and build_site no longer calls it. The existing test_an_older_summary_asks_github_once_per_base_branch passes unchanged.
Both walks keep a record of what they visited, so a cycle in recorded bases, from summaries that disagree, ends the walk rather than looping.
A pull request alone gets an empty list, and the page then shows its title line as before; test_each_page_lists_the_pull_requests_beneath_and_above_it checks a lone pull request gets [].
A pull request known only as a base, with no summary on the site, gets an empty url; the page links it to GitHub instead.

files.note: One new test builds a stack with a branch in it and checks the rows every page gets.

checks.text: The bottom, middle, and top of the stack each list all four pull requests in the same order, with only themselves current. The test passes on this head.

groups.title: The sidebar: stack rows and a Versions list
groups.kicker: The renderer draws the stack below the header and moves Versions under the sections.
intro: site/src/summary.ts builds the page in the browser from data.json. The sidebar block under the repo#number header now holds the stack rows, or the title when there is no stack, and the projects. The head-and-base line is gone.

Versions moves below the section list as a <details> element that starts closed. Each head gets a line with its short SHA and when it was published, formatted in the reader's own time zone from the at time the deploy already wrote.

files.note: Adds stackList, rewrites headsList, and rearranges the sidebar.

checks.text: at is the commit time of the head's summary on the ref, in Unix seconds, so it is when that version was published, not when its commit was made.
A stack of one is impossible from the build, which returns [] instead, but the check keeps an older payload with no stack rendering its title.
Versions now ends the sidebar, after the section list.

files.note: Types the new stack rows and the at time on each head.
Styles the stack rows, with titles wrapping to two lines, and the Versions list, in both themes.
Compiled from site/src/summary.ts by npm run build; the test suite fails when it differs from the source.

groups.title: Documentation
groups.kicker: Two sentences describe the sidebar's stack.
intro: The CLI reference and the summarize-pr skill now say that a summary's page lists the pull requests in its stack.
